questions.article: The Value of a Human Being
questions.q: How does the editorial say “abundant gratitude” (Shukr-e Kaseer) is reached?
options: By repeating words of thanks many times
Not quite. The article says: By discovering God’s universal bounties and reflecting on them as if made for oneself.
By giving up worldly comforts
Not quite. The article says: By discovering God’s universal bounties and reflecting on them as if made for oneself.
By discovering God’s universal bounties and reflecting on them as if made for oneself
Yes. This “personalising” brings what he calls thrilling shukr.
By comparing oneself with those who have less
Not quite. The article says: By discovering God’s universal bounties and reflecting on them as if made for oneself.
questions.rationale: “First you have to discover the universal bounties of God Almighty upon man, and then you have to reflect on what these mean to you personally… Personalise them.”

questions.article: The Value of a Human Being
questions.q: Why, according to the editorial, do even gifted and admired people fall into despair?
options: They have too little leisure
Not quite. The article says: They let the one per cent that is negative outweigh the ninety-nine per cent that is positive, and miss their own worth.
They let the one per cent that is negative outweigh the ninety-nine per cent that is positive, and miss their own worth
Correct. “Change your thinking, and you will discover your true value.”
They were not taught religion as children
Not quite. The article says: They let the one per cent that is negative outweigh the ninety-nine per cent that is positive, and miss their own worth.
They are envied by those around them
Not quite. The article says: They let the one per cent that is negative outweigh the ninety-nine per cent that is positive, and miss their own worth.
questions.rationale: “They forget the 99% positive things they still have in their life and let the negative 1% overwhelm them… every person is born as a hero but his pessimistic way of thinking makes him valueless in his own eyes.”

questions.q: What price, according to the article, must a believer be ready to pay for peace?
options: To bear harm without retaliating, so that constructive work can go on
Right. Positive action in place of reaction.
To leave his home and community
Not quite. The article says: To bear harm without retaliating, so that constructive work can go on.
To give up his beliefs
Not quite. The article says: To bear harm without retaliating, so that constructive work can go on.
To pay those who trouble him
Not quite. The article says: To bear harm without retaliating, so that constructive work can go on.
questions.rationale: “He must suffer all the harm and injustice done to him without making any attempt either to retaliate… The believer has to be willing to pay this price so that his pursuance of constructive ends should proceed unhampered.”

questions.q: When commanded to bow before Adam, the angels obeyed and Satan refused. What two ways of acting does the article see in this?
options: Strength versus weakness
Not quite. The article says: Getting on with one’s work without confrontation, versus the “politics of opposition” driven by ego.
Getting on with one’s work without confrontation, versus the “politics of opposition” driven by ego
Yes. The remedy offered is the “politics of patience.”
Blind obedience versus free thought
Not quite. The article says: Getting on with one’s work without confrontation, versus the “politics of opposition” driven by ego.
Worship versus worldly work
Not quite. The article says: Getting on with one’s work without confrontation, versus the “politics of opposition” driven by ego.
questions.rationale: “To focus on one’s work without confronting the authorities is the method of the angels. And confronting the authorities… fired by the ‘politics of opposition’, is the method of Satan.”

questions.q: When we look at the stars we see light that left them long ago. How does the article use this fact?
options: Eyesight is not to be trusted at all
Not quite. The article says: Much of what we accept is known indirectly, so God too can be known through His signs.
Much of what we accept is known indirectly, so God too can be known through His signs
Well reasoned. Things are known by their effects.
The stars we see no longer exist
Not quite. The article says: Much of what we accept is known indirectly, so God too can be known through His signs.
God lives beyond the farthest stars
Not quite. The article says: Much of what we accept is known indirectly, so God too can be known through His signs.
questions.rationale: “When all the things of this world are accepted on the basis of indirect evidence, why is it that the presence of God should not be accepted on the same basis?”

questions.q: Elephants and tigers almost never fight each other. What lesson for human beings does the article draw from animals’ ways of protecting themselves?
options: Avoid needless confrontation and keep to one’s own constructive work – this is pragmatism, not cowardice
Exactly. Animals do it by instinct; we must do it by choice.
Weak creatures should live in fear
Not quite. The article says: Avoid needless confrontation and keep to one’s own constructive work – this is pragmatism, not cowardice.
It is best to strike first
Not quite. The article says: Avoid needless confrontation and keep to one’s own constructive work – this is pragmatism, not cowardice.
Only the strong survive
Not quite. The article says: Avoid needless confrontation and keep to one’s own constructive work – this is pragmatism, not cowardice.
questions.rationale: “They teach us humans that we, too, should avoid unnecessary confrontation with others, and, instead, should focus on our own growth.”

questions.q: What led Louis Braille to invent his system of reading?
options: A teacher’s instructions at school
Not quite. The article says: Losing his sight, which made him discover the power of touch in the fingertips.
Losing his sight, which made him discover the power of touch in the fingertips
Yes. A loss opened a new opportunity.
A book he had read before he went blind
Not quite. The article says: Losing his sight, which made him discover the power of touch in the fingertips.
A machine in his father’s workshop
Not quite. The article says: Losing his sight, which made him discover the power of touch in the fingertips.
questions.rationale: “After losing his vision… he discovered the power of touch, which is inherent in the finger-tip… ‘disabled’ persons are actually ‘differently-abled’!”

questions.q: One friend took a stone on the road for glass; the other, a jeweller, knew it for a diamond. What does the article say this teaches about truth?
options: Truth is whatever one’s own tradition holds
Not quite. The article says: A lover of truth recognises it wherever it is, inside his own circle or outside it.
A lover of truth recognises it wherever it is, inside his own circle or outside it
Right. Knowing only one’s own “necklace” is not enough.
Valuable things are found by chance
Not quite. The article says: A lover of truth recognises it wherever it is, inside his own circle or outside it.
Only experts can know the truth
Not quite. The article says: A lover of truth recognises it wherever it is, inside his own circle or outside it.
questions.rationale: “A real jeweller is one who recognizes a diamond wherever he sees it. In the same way a lover of truth is one who recognizes truth wherever it is.”

questions.q: After the first revelation the Prophet came home shaken. How did Khadija respond?
options: She reassured him that no harm would come to one who spoke the truth and helped the poor and distressed
Yes. The article gives this as an example of women’s gift for calming and reconciling.
She doubted what he had seen
Not quite. The article says: She reassured him that no harm would come to one who spoke the truth and helped the poor and distressed.
She asked him to tell no one
Not quite. The article says: She reassured him that no harm would come to one who spoke the truth and helped the poor and distressed.
She took him at once to the leaders of Makkah
Not quite. The article says: She reassured him that no harm would come to one who spoke the truth and helped the poor and distressed.
questions.rationale: “She did her best to assure him that no harm would come to him as he always spoke the truth, helped the poor and those in distress, and invariably treated others with respect.”

questions.q: What positive part do our unlimited desires play, according to the article?
options: They are a foretaste pointing to Paradise, and can move us to the deeds that earn it
Well read. This world cannot fulfil them.
They are a weakness to be rooted out
Not quite. The article says: They are a foretaste pointing to Paradise, and can move us to the deeds that earn it.
They prove that man is never to be satisfied anywhere
Not quite. The article says: They are a foretaste pointing to Paradise, and can move us to the deeds that earn it.
They show what we should own in this life
Not quite. The article says: They are a foretaste pointing to Paradise, and can move us to the deeds that earn it.
questions.rationale: “These desires are actually an introduction to paradise in advance… This world is only for man to prove himself worthy for an entry into paradise.”
